Lessons.Title: Solving Problems with Systems of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: interpret systems of inequalities with strict and inclusive boundaries, test whether a point on an intersection edge counts as a solution and identify missing contextual assumptions. Original independent Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition U02:L25, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/25/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). The source specifically distinguishes included and excluded boundary points, not merely approximate graph shading.

Original charity event model: muffins m sell for $3 each and cookies c sell for $2 each. A booth can prepare at least 20 items and has a maximum ingredient budget of $60 in this simplified equal-price resource model. Conditions m+c≥20, 3m+2c≤60, m,c nonnegative integers. A pair (10,10) satisfies item count 20 and cost $50, and (20,0) lies on both inclusive boundaries.

Contrast a strict requirement 3m+2c<60: pair (20,0) no longer satisfies the cost condition because it equals 60. Pair (15,10) has cost $65 and item count 25, so fails in both inclusive and strict variants. An exact line may be included for ≥ while a second line excluded for <; show solid/dashed patterns independently.

Student task: create one graph for inclusive system and another after a strict change, label feasible points, explain the status of (20,0) and a non-integer point and propose an additional relevant resource constraint. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 each for complete system, boundary status, numerical testing and explanatory graph/assumption critique.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inclusive boundary
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a solid line and include equality points.
KeyConcepts.Example: At m=20,c=0, item count 20 and cost 60 meet inclusive limits.

KeyConcepts.Title: Strict boundary
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a dashed line and explicitly test the edge.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intersect restrictions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every inequality and the count domain apply at the same time.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test item count, cost and nonnegativity separately.
KeyConcepts.Example: (15,10) gives 25 items but $65, so not feasible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test a point inside the feasible set
WorkedExamples.Question: For m=10,c=10, check both constraints.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish inclusive versus strict
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (20,0) feasible for cost ≤60 and cost <60?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: The boundary must switch from solid to dashed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a superficially abundant plan
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (15,10) feasible?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret the stated inequality system, use valid domains and independently verify each numerical case.
Steps: Point lies outside the budget half-plane.
WorkedExamples.Check: One satisfied condition cannot compensate for another failure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a solid line for a strict limit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That suggests the excluded equality points count.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring integer restrictions in item counts
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Fractions of a muffin may be algebraically plotted but physically unsupported.

SummaryPoints: Boundary inclusion can differ between constraints in one system.
At (20,0), $60 is allowed under ≤60 but not under <60.
A valid real-world plan satisfies every inequality and domain constraint.
Teacher evaluates diagrams, symbols and contextual argument.
